q-59711:
The object is accelerating when its acceleration is positive. In a speed-time graph, the acceleration is given by the slope of the line. So, we need to find the times for which the slope is positive.

We see from the graph that the slope is positive from $t=0\,\text{s}$ to $t=30\,\text{s}.$ Therefore, the object is accelerating in this time interval.

q-108462:
The motorcycle is accelerating when its acceleration is positive. In a speed-time graph, the acceleration is given by the slope of the line. So, we need to find the times for which the slope is positive.

We see from the graph that the slope is positive from $t=30\,\text{s}$ to $t=60\,\text{s}.$ Therefore, the $250\text{cc}$ motorcycle is accelerating in this time interval.

q-59760:
We start the first line from the point $(0,0),$ since the particle starts from rest. Then, because the acceleration is $5\,{\text{km/h}}^{2},$ we draw a line with slope $5.$ 

However, because the particle is only accelerating for the first $4$ hours, we stop the line at $t=4.$ At this time, the particle's speed has increased by $4\cdot 5=20\text{ km/h}.$ So, the first line segment goes from $(0,0)$ to $(4,20).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945962/assets/cf0471f38486963f4237b4fab7c1cd109d02cc2d7ac3e30990831654f04c5b11.png)

The particle then travels at a constant speed for the next $6$ hours. So, the speed remains at $20\,\text{km/h}$ for the next $6$ hours, until $t=4+6=10.$

So, the second line segment stops at the point $(10,20).$ The final graph is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945962/assets/fae4c7d8cfc79dd70041ebd697226408a5cdd0676ad2ddfaad1500ea1ba0a76e.png)

q-108567:
We start the first line from the point $(0,0),$ since the particle starts from rest. Then, because the acceleration is $1\,{\text{km/h}}^{2},$ we draw a line with slope $1.$ 

However, because the particle is only accelerating for the first $3$ hours, we stop the line at $t=3.$ At this time, the particle's speed has increased by $1\cdot 3=3\,\text{km/h}.$ So, the first line segment goes from $(0,0)$ to $(3,3).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945962/assets/7a9fd32e5705860064e597fcf9308fee457063e060d3adede260f109ca488201.png)

The particle then travels at a constant speed for the next $3$ hours. So, the speed remains at $3\,\text{km/h}$ for the next $3$ hours, until $t=3+3=6.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945962/assets/e4c7e47150bf1c205c243c6fa1d0f0e24b7a69f27a8461791d495eb7487cf4f3.png)

After $t=3,$ the particle has an acceleration of $0.5\,{\text{km/h}}^{2},$ so the slope of the third line segment is $0.5.$ The third line segment stops after $3$ hours. To figure out the velocity at this moment, we need to find the equation for the third line segment.

Since the third line segment passes through the point $(6,3)$ and has a slope of $0.5,$ we can use point-slope form to write the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}v-{v}_{1} & =m(t-{t}_{1}) \\ v-3 & =0.5(t-6) \\ v-3 & =0.5t-3 \\ v & =0.5t\end{aligned}
$$

The third line segment stops when $t=6+3=9$ hours, and the velocity at this moment is

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =0.5t \\ v & =0.5(9) \\ v & =4.5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the third line segment stops at the point $(9,4.5).$ The final graph is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13945962/assets/a3fb0b9ebb6ef907a77c3d8ce139802dbd72fab04ea0bfc5db57e9f028c263b9.png)

q-70903:
To find the slope of the tangent at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡10}+3{x}^{2}\,.
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=3} & ={(\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡10}+3{x}^{2})|}_{x=3} \\  & =\frac{3}{3\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡10}+3\cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡10}+27\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-28266:
In this case, the area of the right triangle is

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot BC.
$$

We are given that $\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A)=5.$ Notice that relative to $∠A,$ we have expressions for the lengths of the opposite side $\overset{―}{BC}$ and adjacent side $\overset{―}{AC}.$ Hence, we can use the tangent ratio to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A) & =\frac{BC}{AC} \\ 5 & =\frac{2x+4}{x-1} \\ 5(x-1) & =2x+4 \\ 5x-5 & =2x+4 \\ 3x & =9 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the side lengths are

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =2x+4=2(3)+4=10, \\ AC & =x-1=3-1=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of $△ABC$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot BC \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 10 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

q-76773:
In this case, the area of the right triangle is

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}AB\cdot BC.
$$

We are given that $m∠A={30}^{∘}.$ Notice that relative to $∠A,$ we have expressions for the lengths of the opposite side $\overset{―}{BC}$ and adjacent side $\overset{―}{AB}.$ Hence, we can use the tangent ratio to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A) & =\frac{BC}{AB} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡({30}^{∘}) & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\,x}{x+4} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\,x}{x+4} \\ \sqrt{3}(x+4) & =3\cdot \sqrt{3}\,x \\ \sqrt{3}\,x+4\sqrt{3} & =3\sqrt{3}\,x \\ -2\sqrt{3}\,x & =-4\sqrt{3} \\ x & =\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{3}} \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the side lengths are 

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =\sqrt{3}\,x=\sqrt{3}(2)=2\sqrt{3}, \\ AB & =x+4=2+4=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of $△ABC$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot AB\cdot BC \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot 2\sqrt{3} \\  & =6\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-124475:
In this case, the area of the right triangle is

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}AC\cdot AB.
$$

We are given that $m∠B={60}^{∘}.$ Notice that relative to $∠B,$ we have expressions for the lengths of the opposite side $\overset{―}{AC}$ and adjacent side $\overset{―}{AB}.$ Hence, we can use the tangent ratio to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(m∠A) & =\frac{AC}{AB} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡({60}^{∘}) & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}\,x}{x+2} \\ \sqrt{3} & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}\,x}{x+2} \\ \sqrt{3}(x+2) & =2\sqrt{3}\,x \\ \sqrt{3}\,x+2\sqrt{3} & =2\sqrt{3}\,x \\ 2\sqrt{3} & =\sqrt{3}\,x \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the side lengths are 

$$
\begin{aligned}AC & =2\sqrt{3}\,x=2\sqrt{3}\cdot 2=4\sqrt{3}, \\ AB & =x+2=2+2=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of $△ABC$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot AC\cdot AB \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\sqrt{3}\cdot 4 \\  & =8\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-18688:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the second equation by $10,$ as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}b=2a-1 &  \\ 1.5a+0.5b=2.5 & |\,\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}b=2a-1 \\ 15a+5b=25\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the first equation is already solved for $b:$

$$
b=2a-1
$$

Now, to find the value of $a,$ we can substitute $b=2a-1$ into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}15a+5(2a-1) & =25 \\ 15a+10a-5 & =25 \\ 25a & =30 \\ a & =\frac{30}{25} \\ a & =1.2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $a=1.2$ into the  first equation to get:

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =2(1.2)-1 \\  & =2.4-1 \\  & =1.4\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $a=1.2$ and $b=1.4.$

q-112561:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the second equation by $10,$ as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+3y=7 &  \\ 0.5x+0.4y=0.2 & |\,\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x+3y=7 \\ 5x+4y=2\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we multiply the  first equation by $-5,$ then we will get a $-5x$ term that can cancel with the $5x$ term in the second equation:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+3y=7 & |\,\times (-5) \\ 5x+4y=2\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}-5x-15y=-35 \\ 5x+4y=2\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $x$-variable and allows us to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}-\cancel{5x}-15y & =-35 \\ \cancel{5x}+4y & =2 \\ (-15y+4y) & =(-33) \\ -11y & =-33 \\ y & =3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $y=3$ into the equation $x+3y=7$ to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x+3y & =7 \\ x+3(3) & =7 \\ x+9 & =7 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-2,\,y=3.$ So,

$$
x+y=(-2)+(3)=1.
$$

q-26223:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply both equations by $10,$ as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0.3x-0.1y=0.6 & |\,\times 10 \\ 0.6x+0.8y=0.2 & |\,\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}3x-y=6 \\ 6x+8y=2\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we divide the second equation by $(-2),$ we will get a $-3x$ term in the second equation that can cancel with the $3x$ term in the first equation:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3x-y=6 &  \\ 6x+8y=2 & |\,÷(-2)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}3x-y=6 \\ -3x-4y=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $x$-variable and allows us to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{3x}-y & =6 \\ -\cancel{3x}-4y & =-1 \\ (-y-4y) & =(6-1) \\ -5y & =5 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $y=-1$ into the equation $3x-y=6$ to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-y & =6 \\ 3x-(-1) & =6 \\ 3x & =5 \\ x & =\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $x=\frac{5}{3}$ and $y=-1.$

q-18720:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the first equation by $100$ and the second equation by $10,$ as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0.36p+1.2q=0.36 & |\times 100 \\ -1.9p-7.6q=3.8 & |\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}36p+120q=36 \\ -19p-76q=38\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we can solve for $p$ in the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-19p-76q & =38 \\ -19p & =76q+38 \\ p & =\frac{76q+38}{-19} \\ p & =-4q-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the value of $q,$ we can substitute $p=-4q-2$ into the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}36p+120q & =36 \\ 36(-4q-2)+120q & =36 \\ -144q-72+120q & =36 \\ -24q & =108 \\ q & =-\frac{108}{24} \\ q & =-4.5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $q=-4.5$ into the equation $p=-4q-2$ to get:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =-4q-2 \\ p & =-4(-4.5)-2 \\ p & =18-2 \\ p & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=16$ and $q=-4.5.$ So, 

$$
p+2q=16+2(-4.5)=16-9=7.
$$

q-18027:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}bc\operatorname{sin}⁡A,
$$

where $∠A$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}с & =AB=26, \\ b & =AC=22, \\ m∠A & ={11}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡{11}^{∘}=0.190\,809,
$$

rounded to six decimal places,  we calculate the area as follows:
 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 22\cdot 26\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{11}^{∘} \\  & =286\cdot (0.190\,809) \\  & ≈54.57,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

q-43339:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}bc\operatorname{sin}⁡A,
$$

where $∠A$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB=5\,\text{ cm}, \\ b & =AC=12\,\text{cm}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate $m∠A$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ 15 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 12\cdot 5\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ 15 & =30\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \frac{15}{30} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡A & =\frac{1}{2} \\ m∠A & ={30}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-72768:
The diagonal $\overset{―}{AC}$ divides the parallelogram into two congruent triangles. Therefore, the area of the parallelogram is twice the area of $△ACB$ (see the illustration below).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13946476/assets/7cfcb5cdf77b4afbf25afd64e37bb33f0ab2c211e09659181bfc16db0ccd2db7.png)

 Computing the area of $△ACB,$ we find
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ACD} & =\frac{1}{2}(18)(8)\operatorname{sin}⁡{70}^{∘} \\  & =72\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{70}^{∘} \\  & ≈67.658,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places. Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABCD} & =2{A}_{ACB} \\  & =2\cdot 67.658 \\  & =135.316.\end{aligned}
$$

So, to the nearest integer, the area of the parallelogram is $135.$

q-72764:
Let's start by finding the area of $△ABD.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△ABD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot AB\cdot AD\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9\cdot 15\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{52}^{∘} \\  & =67.5\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{52}^{∘} \\  & =53.190… \\  & ≈53{\text{ cm}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

The difference of the areas of $△ABD$ and the quadrilateral $ABCD$ gives the area of $△BCD.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△BCD} & ={A}_{△ABD}-{A}_{ABCD} \\  & =53-34 \\  & =19{\text{ cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
